blocks.title: Honors — choosing axes is a decision you defend
blocks.markdown: On an incline, CPA tilts the axes so x runs along the slope and resolves gravity into components. Honors does the same calculation — and then **justifies why that choice was the smart one.** Picking axes isn't a rule handed to you; it's a modeling decision, and a strong analyst can say out loud why it pays off.

## Why tilt the axes?

You *could* keep x horizontal and y vertical. The physics would still be correct. But then **two** forces — the normal force and the slide — would each have x and y parts, and the motion would mix both axes. Messy.

Tilt the axes to match the slope and something clean happens: the object only accelerates **along** the incline, so the whole problem collapses onto one axis. The normal force points straight along the new y (no component to chase), and only **gravity** has to be decomposed:

$$F_{\parallel} = mg\sin\theta \qquad F_{\perp} = mg\cos\theta$$

The decomposition choice isn't about getting a different answer — it's about choosing the frame where the answer is **easiest to defend**. That is the honors move: not just *do* it, but be able to say *why this frame and not the other.*

blocks.title: State your assumptions
blocks.markdown: Your incline result $F_\parallel = mg\sin\theta$ quietly assumes several things: the ramp is **frictionless** (or you've added friction as its own term), the incline is **rigid** and doesn't deform, the angle $\theta$ is measured from the **horizontal**, and the object is a **point** sliding without tipping or rolling. Name these before you trust the number — a stated assumption is a checkable one.

blocks.frame: I chose to tilt my axes along the slope because ___. With horizontal/vertical axes instead, the problem would be harder because ___. One assumption my decomposition rests on is ___.
blocks.prompt: JUSTIFY: For a block on a frictionless ramp, explain why you decomposed gravity along tilted (slope-aligned) axes rather than horizontal/vertical ones. Argue what specifically gets easier, and name one assumption your decomposition depends on.
